rows: Suspected respiratory or cutaneous diphtheria requires prompt public-health notification.
Public-health management includes investigation of cases and close contacts.
Clinical suspicion can trigger action before final laboratory confirmation.
Isolation and infection-control measures may be required.
Laboratory testing supports confirmation and toxigenicity assessment.
Contacts may need risk assessment, testing, vaccination review or prophylaxis.
Case and contact vaccination status should be reviewed.
Clusters and outbreaks require coordinated health-protection action.
A sore throat, skin lesion or travel history does not establish diphtheria.
Decisions require clinical, laboratory, toxigenicity, timing, exposure, vaccination and public-health evidence.
Invasive group A streptococcal disease is serious and requires prompt clinical management.
Public-health teams assess close contacts in community settings.
Contact definitions depend on exposure and timing.
All relevant household contacts should receive information about symptoms requiring urgent attention.
Some close contacts or risk groups may be offered antibiotic chemoprophylaxis.
Nursery, school and childcare settings require setting-specific assessment.
Probable and confirmed cases can both require contact actions.
Surveillance after exposure supports early detection of secondary cases.
A shared setting or sore throat does not establish invasive disease or transmission.
Decisions require case classification, diagnosis date, exposure, risk group, symptoms and public-health evidence.
Botulism is a rare but potentially life-threatening neuroparalytic illness.
Foodborne botulism is treated as a public-health emergency.
Clinical suspicion should prompt urgent specialist advice.
Antitoxin should not be delayed when clinical suspicion is strong.
Laboratory samples should be collected and handled through the reference pathway.
Food histories and associated samples support source investigation.
Wound and iatrogenic botulism require exposure-specific investigation.
Public-health teams should report and coordinate suspected cases.
A neurological symptom or food exposure alone does not establish botulism.
Conclusions require clinical pattern, timing, exposure, laboratory, antitoxin and investigation evidence.
Typhoid and paratyphoid cases require public-health investigation.
The guidance supports identification of infection sources and reduction of secondary transmission.
Cases are notifiable under the health-protection notification framework.
Travel history is important in the risk assessment.
Enhanced surveillance questionnaires support consistent investigation.
Contacts and co-travellers may require targeted assessment or screening.
Microbiological clearance requirements depend on case and risk-group circumstances.
Outbreaks should follow agreed national and local outbreak plans.
Travel to an endemic area or gastrointestinal symptoms do not establish enteric fever.
Decisions require laboratory, symptoms, travel, occupation, contacts, treatment and clearance evidence.
